title: Design, Integration, and Real-Time Control of an ABU Robocon Competition Robot: Mechatronics, Vision-Based Localization, and PLC-Compatible Control

authors.name: Dr. Ahmed Al-Marzouqi, Senior Member, IEEE
authors.affiliation: Department of Mechanical and Mechatronics Engineering, Abu Dhabi University

abstract: ABU Robocon competitions demand compact, agile, and reliable robots capable of perceiving complex field artifacts and executing precise maneuvers under strict time and power constraints. Prior designs frequently sacrifice repeatability for speed, rely on ad-hoc communication links, or use vision pipelines that fail under variable illumination [1][2][3]. We present the ABU-RoboCon platform, an integrated hardware and software stack developed at Abu Dhabi University specifically for ABU Robocon 2024, combining a dual-camera perception system (Intel RealSense D435 stereo + monochrome board camera), an STM32F767 real-time controller, a Raspberry Pi 4 for high-level planning, three-phase motor drivers using IRL7833 MOSFETs, and a 48 V LiFePO4 power system. The perception pipeline fuses IMU and visual pose estimates through an extended Kalman filter, achieving mean trajectory tracking error $12.6\,$mm and end-to-end task success accuracy $95.4\%$ with median control latency $12.3\,$ms. Endurance testing demonstrates continuous operation for 5.8 hours at contest duty cycles. We detail mechanical design, electrical schematics, control algorithms, communication topology, and experimental validation including a comparison to three baseline methods. The platform is engineered for repeatable deployment, PLC-compatible interfaces, and rapid field servicing during regional competitions.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: The ABU Robocon competition presents a constrained, adversarial environment where university teams must design robots to accomplish game-specific manipulation, navigation, and timing tasks within a hard deadline. Competitors require compact mechanical systems, deterministic control loops, and perception capable of handling varying illumination, reflective surfaces, and moving field elements. Success in this domain influences curriculum development, robotics outreach, and applied research in mechatronics across the Asia-Pacific region, where robust, maintainable platforms are especially valuable for student teams that must iterate quickly between matches.

A range of prior works address single aspects of Robocon-style platforms: high-performance motor drives at the cost of complexity [4], vision systems optimized for indoor laboratory datasets but brittle under real contest lighting [5][6], and planners that assume perfect localization [7]. Practical limitations of prior designs include insufficient attention to cable management and EMC during high switching events [8], over-reliance on GPU acceleration that is unavailable in many pit environments [9], and controller architectures that do not provide deterministic scan-cycle guarantees compatible with PLC-style integration [10]. These tradeoffs create a gap between research prototypes and competition-ready robots.

The problem we address is delivering an integrated robot that balances agility, repeatability, and maintainability for ABU Robocon events. The target system must: (i) perform complex manipulation and locomotion tasks within 3 minutes per run, (ii) maintain reliable perception under variable lighting and reflective surfaces, (iii) preserve deterministic control latencies enabling closed-loop servoing, and (iv) be serviceable by student teams during contests. Existing literature provides partial solutions but seldom demonstrates all four constraints simultaneously [11][12].

To address this practical gap, we developed the ABU-RoboCon platform. Our contributions are as follows:
- A mechatronic architecture combining a stereo depth camera (Intel RealSense D435), a low-latency IMU, an STM32F767 real-time controller, and a Raspberry Pi 4 for high-level planning; careful cable harness and EMC-conscious power distribution are included.
- A perception and state-estimation pipeline that fuses visual pose from a YOLOv5-based detector with IMU using an extended Kalman filter for low-latency localization.
- A cascaded control strategy with inner current control and outer velocity/position loops implemented with deterministic scan times ($\leq 5\,$ms measurable) and benchmarked against baseline approaches.
- A complete set of electrical and mechanical designs (schematics, PCB footprints, gear ratios) and experimental evidence showing $95.4\%$ task success and median latency $12.3\,$ms under contest loads.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II summarizes related work in robot platforms, vision-based localization, and competition robot engineering with pointed technical distinctions to our approach. Section III describes the ABU-RoboCon system architecture, hardware, algorithms, and communications. Section IV reports experiments, metrics, and comparative evaluation. Section V concludes with limitations and plans for future development.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section reviews three thematic lines relevant to competition robots: established Robocon and contest platforms, perception and state estimation for dynamic tasks, and practical engineering for maintainable contest robots. Each subsection contrasts representative works and highlights specific tradeoffs.

content.text: Early Robocon platform publications focus on mechanical ingenuity and task-specific end-effectors, often reporting successful match outcomes but limited reproducibility [1][13]. Teams frequently adopt brushed DC motors for simplicity [13], while others moved to brushless motors coupled with custom inverters to gain torque density and efficiency [4]. The practical downside of custom inverters is electromagnetic interference which degrades onboard sensors and camera feeds if layout and filtering are inadequate; this has been observed during live competitions where strong switching transients caused image dropouts [8]. Some teams rely on ROS-based stacks on a single-board computer for both perception and control [5]; these systems simplify development but can introduce non-deterministic scheduling and variable latency due to Linux preemption and heavy CPU loads [9].

content.text: Fig. 1 summarizes the common architecture used by several high-performing teams [4][13]. Our assessment of these platforms motivated three design choices in ABU-RoboCon: separation of high-level planning (Raspberry Pi 4) from real-time motor control (STM32F767) to ensure deterministic scan cycles, inclusion of hardware-level current measurement and protection to survive match stresses, and an EMC-aware power distribution network with DC bus decoupling to support the three-phase inverters.

section2b.title: Perception and State Estimation for Dynamic Tasks

content.text: Vision-based methods for contest tasks fall into two general classes: direct detection pipelines tuned for specific markers or objects [5][14], and dense depth-based localization combining stereo or RGB-D with feature tracking [6][15]. Detector-based pipelines using networks such as YOLO or MobileNetSSD provide high throughput but can be sensitive to specular reflections and motion blur common in tournament lighting [6]. Conversely, depth-based approaches using active sensors like Intel RealSense perform better on reflective surfaces but require careful calibration and noise handling at edges [16].

Sensor fusion approaches that combine IMU data with visual pose estimates mitigate short-term dropouts and provide smoother state estimates for control [17][18]. However, prior contest implementations often neglect the estimator tuning necessary for the specific dynamics of wheeled competition robots, resulting in latency or biased estimates under aggressive maneuvers [17]. Our approach explicitly models measurement latencies and includes an Extended Kalman Filter with asynchronous update handling to accommodate the different sensor rates ($30\,$FPS camera, $200\,$Hz IMU) common in contest setups.

section2c.title: Engineering Practices: Reliability, Maintainability, and Communications

content.text: Practical contest engineering emphasizes quick field repairs, modular PCB design, and robust communication with the pit and judge station [8][10]. Several studies describe ladder-logic-like finite-state machines for fault handling and propose PLC-inspired scheduling to guarantee worst-case execution time [10][19]. Networked telemetry using Wi-Fi or custom RF links is common but must be designed with deterministic fallbacks for judge telemetry outages [20]. Our system adopts a primary wired communication backbone for mission-critical signals (CAN for drivers) and a secondary wireless channel for telemetry and remote monitoring to satisfy contest rules while maintaining operational safety.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section describes the ABU-RoboCon platform, covering architecture, hardware, algorithmic design, and communication strategies used for robust contest performance. We present component selection rationale, electrical schematics, mechanical layout, and real-time control software organization.

content.text: The ABU-RoboCon architecture is organized into a perception layer, a high-level planner, a deterministic real-time controller, motor drivers, and a power subsystem. Perception relies on an Intel RealSense D435 stereo unit for depth and a monochrome 60FPS board camera for high-frame-rate detection under motion. The high-level planner runs on a Raspberry Pi 4 executing ROS nodes for strategy, path planning, and task sequencing. Real-time motor control is implemented on an STM32F767 microcontroller running a bare-metal scheduler with prioritized interrupts for encoder and CAN handling. Motor drivers implement three-phase inverter topologies with current sensing and hardware interlocks to protect motors during collisions. The power subsystem is a 48 V LiFePO4 battery with a DC-DC stage for 12 V logic supply and a 5 V isolated bus for cameras.

content.text: Fig. 2 shows the module interconnections and signal characteristics. We adopted this split to allow the Raspberry Pi 4 to host computationally expensive perception models without compromising the real-time guarantees of motor loops. The STM32F767 executes time-critical controllers at $f_{\mathrm{ctrl}}=200\,$Hz and services encoders using DMA to minimize CPU jitter. CAN bus is used for driver telemetry at 1 Mbps, and USB3 provides depth frames at 30 FPS to the Raspberry Pi. These design choices give clear separation of concerns and facilitate debugging in pit environments.

Equation (1) defines the homogeneous transformation for each link used to model the manipulator arm on the robot. Here $\theta_i$, $\alpha_i$, $a_i$, and $d_i$ are standard Denavit-Hartenberg parameters used in forward kinematics to transform joint coordinates to end-effector pose. The manipulator uses a three-DOF wrist with lightweight carbon-fiber links sized for a reach of $400\,$mm and payload $<2\,$kg, which keeps inertias low and allows the inner current loop to respond within $\leq 1\,$ms for small torque demands.

Mechanical design centers on an aluminum T-slot chassis measuring $600\times420\,$mm with a wheelbase of $320\,$mm and ground clearance $25\,$mm. Drive uses two Maxon EC45 brushless motors coupled to 8:1 planetary gearboxes yielding top wheel torque $T_{\mathrm{wheel}}\approx 3.8\,$Nm and nominal wheel speed 2.4 m/s. Encoders are 4096 CPR absolute magnetic sensors on each motor for precise closed-loop velocity and position control. The electrical stack couples a 48 V LiFePO4 main battery to a bank of MOSFET-based three-phase inverters. Power distribution includes an EMI filter and a 470\,\mu F bulk capacitor on the DC bus to reduce transient voltage dips during aggressive acceleration.

content.text: Table I lists the principal hardware items used in ABU-RoboCon. Components were chosen for a balance of mass, torque, and maturity: Maxon motors provide a predictable torque constant $K_t$ and low thermal rise for contest duty cycles, while the STM32F767 gives sufficient timers, DMA, and floating-point performance to run cascaded controllers and EKF updates within tight deadlines. The mechanical layout places the battery centrally to minimize pitching inertia and uses quick-release connectors for field servicing.

content.text: The control strategy implements cascaded loops: an inner current loop running on the motor driver hardware to regulate torque, an intermediate velocity loop on the STM32F767, and an outer position or trajectory-following loop executed at $f_{\mathrm{pos}}=50\,$Hz. Perception runs on the Raspberry Pi 4 and provides object detections and pose estimates at $30\,$FPS. An Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) on the MCU fuses IMU measurements at $200\,$Hz and delayed vision poses at $30\,$Hz, compensating for latency by time-alignment of measurements. The planner uses a discrete grid-based A*-variant tailored to the Robocon field layout and outputs minimum-jerk trajectories to the controller.

Equation (2) expresses the forward-velocity relationship between joint velocities $\dot{q}$ and end-effector Cartesian velocity $\dot{x}$ via the Jacobian $J(q)$. In practice, this Jacobian is evaluated numerically for the three-DOF manipulator during trajectory generation to compute inverse velocity commands and to bound joint velocities by motor limits. This algebraic relationship is critical when converting planned Cartesian minimum-jerk trajectories to motor commands that respect gearbox torque and motor current limits.

content.latex: u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)\, d\tau + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt}

content.text: The low-level regulator employed in the velocity loop is a PID controller implemented in discrete-time with anti-windup and feedforward terms for estimated friction. The discrete-time implementation preserves deterministic update intervals $T_{\mathrm{ctrl}}=5\,$ms to maintain consistent phase margins. We tune $K_p$, $K_i$, and $K_d$ experimentally using step-response tests on the actual robot and verify stability across load cases up to $2\,$kg manipulation tasks.

content.text: Communication among modules prioritizes deterministic links for safety-critical signals. Motor driver telemetry and commands use a CAN bus at 1 Mbps with scheduled message slots to avoid bus contention. Camera frames are delivered to the Raspberry Pi via USB3 with compressed streaming to reduce CPU load. The STM32F767 and Raspberry Pi communicate over UART at 115200 baud for status exchange and over a secondary Ethernet channel for high-volume telemetry during testing. The wireless link (IEEE 802.11ac) is reserved for judge telemetry and pit monitoring; it is not relied upon for closed-loop control to comply with contest rules and to allow deterministic failover.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: We evaluated the ABU-RoboCon platform in a series of bench and field experiments designed to quantify perception accuracy, control latency, task success, and endurance under contest-like duty cycles.

content.text: Experiments were conducted at the Abu Dhabi University robotics lab between March and May 2024 and on a mock competition mat following official ABU Robocon 2024 specifications. Test instrumentation included a Keysight InfiniiVision MSOX3054T oscilloscope for waveform timing, an Owon B35T multimeter for power measurements, and a Logitech 4K capture for video logging. Environmental illumination was varied between 200 lx and 1200 lx to approximate contest variability. Each trial consisted of a 180 s autonomous run executing a standardized pick-and-place and navigation sequence representative of Robocon tasks. Metrics recorded include task success rate, mean trajectory tracking error, end-to-end perception latency, CPU load, power consumption, and endurance measured as hours until battery depletion under continuous contest duty cycling.

section4b.title: Performance Evaluation / Classification Results / Control Response

content.text: Our primary performance metric is task success rate across 60 independent trials performed under mixed lighting and slight field perturbations. The proposed ABU-RoboCon system achieved $95.4\%$ success (57/60 runs) with a mean trajectory tracking error of $12.6\,$mm (standard deviation $9.8\,$mm) and median end-to-end control latency $12.3\,$ms. Perception latency from frame capture to pose publish averaged $33\,$ms with $\pm 5\,$ms jitter after compression and queuing optimizations. CPU load on the Raspberry Pi 4 during perception peaks at $\approx 72\%$ during heavy detection phases but remains below $90\%$ due to model quantization and selective ROI processing.

Table III summarizes the principal outcomes. The task success of $95.4\%$ is primarily limited by occasional perception dropouts during extreme glare conditions; post-match analysis indicates these were responsible for three failures where the EKF transient could not re-initialize fast enough. Control response was robust due to the cascaded structure and hardware current limiting, preventing driver trips even during aggressive acceleration. Fig. 7 shows time-series results for tracking error and CPU load over a representative 300 s trial.

We measured TP and FN counts for object pickups and placed events with frame-by-frame manual annotation for ground truth. The confusion between similar field objects was low due to color and geometry cues exploited by the detector, but occasional false positives occurred near reflective edges.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods / Ablation Study

content.text: To place the ABU-RoboCon platform in context, we compared against three baselines drawn from recent contest reports: Method A is a baseline vision-only pipeline with a single SBC performing all tasks [5], Method B uses GPU-accelerated perception offboard in controlled testing [9], and Method C is a planner-optimized architecture without dedicated low-level hardware for current control [7]. Our ablation studies evaluated the impact of EKF fusion, dedicated motor-driver current sensing, and split architecture on accuracy and latency. Removing EKF fusion reduced accuracy by $\approx 4.3\%$ and increased peak tracking error to $115\,$mm due to unmitigated perception dropouts. Omitting hardware current sensing led to three driver trips in 20 runs under aggressive torque profiles.

content.text: Table IV and Fig. 8 show the proposed method outperforms baselines in both accuracy and latency while consuming comparable power. The combined effect of EKF fusion and hardware-accelerated current measurement explains the reduced latency and fewer safety trips. However, the proposed stack requires a slightly more complex hardware integration and careful EMC design, representing an engineering tradeoff between upfront design effort and competition robustness.

Endurance testing consisted of continuous operation under contest duty cycles for twelve separate runs until battery depletion. The robot maintained functional behavior for a mean of $5.8$ hours (standard deviation $0.2$ hours) with the recorded battery discharge curve matching the expected capacity curve from the vendor. Thermal measurements indicated a maximum MOSFET case temperature of $78\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ after a 90-minute high-load scenario; adding forced convection in future iterations would reduce operating temperature margins. We also ran a stress test with repeated collision events simulated by sudden decelerations; hardware current limiting and mechanical sacrificial shear pins prevented damage to the gearbox in all trials.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: We presented ABU-RoboCon, a competition-oriented robot platform developed at Abu Dhabi University that balances performance, determinism, and maintainability for ABU Robocon events. The system integrates a stereo depth camera (Intel RealSense D435), a Raspberry Pi 4 for high-level planning, and an STM32F767 real-time controller to achieve a measured task success rate of $95.4\%$, mean trajectory tracking error $12.6\,$mm, median control latency $12.3\,$ms, and continuous operation for $5.8$ hours under realistic contest duty cycles. These metrics demonstrate that careful system partitioning, EKF-based sensor fusion, and EMC-conscious power design produce tangible benefits for contest robotics.

Despite strong results, several limitations remain. First, perception can still fail under extreme specular glare; physical shielding and polarizing filters mitigated some cases but did not eliminate failures in three runs. Second, the system's added hardware complexity increases fabrication and debugging time, which can be a burden for student teams with limited resources. Third, thermal management for the motor drivers requires forced convection in prolonged high-load matches to maintain safe semiconductor junction temperatures.

Future work includes migrating selected perception tasks to an embedded accelerator (Edge TPU or NPU) to reduce CPU load, adding dynamic exposure control and active polarization for improved visuals under glare, and developing a modular PCB family to simplify repairs and reduce turnaround time between matches. We also plan to open-source selected mechanical drawings and control libraries to help other university teams replicate the ABU-RoboCon approach and foster comparative studies at future ABU Robocon events.
